articles.title: How to Estimate Investment Growth With Monthly Additions
articles.excerpt: How a starting amount and regular monthly additions grow at a steady return, the formula, a worked ten-year example, and why the early years and the start date matter.
blocks: An investment with regular additions grows in two ways: the money you already have earns a return, and each new addition starts earning too. Compound growth is what makes the second half of a long period add much more than the first. This guide shows the formula for a starting amount plus monthly additions, a worked ten-year example, and what changes the answer most. The Investment Calculator does the sums, shows a year-by-year table and writes out the steps.

The future value of money is how much a present amount will grow to when it earns interest. Money invested at time zero grows by a factor of (1 + i) every period, so after n periods it is worth the starting amount times (1 + i)^n. Regular additions are each treated the same way for the time they stay invested, and the sum of all of them is a standard formula. An online calculator from the US investor education site Investor.gov asks for exactly these inputs: an initial investment, a monthly contribution, a rate and a time.

Monthly rate i = yearly return ÷ 12 ÷ 100
Number of months n = years × 12
Balance = P × (1 + i)^n + C × ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i

P is the starting amount and C is the monthly addition. This version puts each addition at the end of its month. If you add at the start of each month, every addition earns one extra month, so that second part is multiplied by (1 + i).

Start with ₹1,00,000 and add ₹5,000 a month for 10 years at 12% a year. The monthly rate is 0.01 and n is 120, so (1.01)^120 is about 3.3004. The starting amount grows to 1,00,000 × 3.3004 = ₹3,30,038.69. The additions grow to 5,000 × (3.3004 − 1) ÷ 0.01 = ₹11,50,193.45. The balance is ₹14,80,232.14. The money you actually put in is 1,00,000 + 5,000 × 120 = ₹7,00,000, so the estimated returns are ₹7,80,232.14, more than the amount you put in.

Time: at the same return, 5 years gives ₹5,90,018.02, while 10 years gives ₹14,80,232.14. The second five years add far more than the first, because the balance is larger
The start date: money invested early has the longest time to grow
The return: a higher return compounds faster, but a return you cannot rely on is not a plan
Timing: additions at the start of each month give ₹14,91,734.07 in the example, about ₹11,500 more than additions at the end

The calculator also lists the balance at the end of every year next to the money put in. Look at how the gap between the two columns widens. In the first year the returns are small, because there is little invested, while in the last year the balance earns more in one year than the early years earned in total. If you change the monthly addition or the return, the table shows straight away which years change most, which is a quick way to test what is worth saving or waiting for.

The calculation assumes the same return every month. Real investments rise and fall, and a return of 12% a year on average does not mean 12% in every year. It also ignores fees, taxes and inflation, which reduce what the money can buy. The result is an illustration of how compounding works, not a prediction or advice about any particular investment.

Treating an expected return as a guaranteed one
Forgetting that inflation reduces the real value of the final balance
Using the yearly return as the monthly rate instead of dividing by 12
Ignoring costs and taxes on the returns

In the calculator, enter the starting amount, the monthly addition, the expected yearly return and the number of years, and choose whether additions are made at the start or end of each month. The answer shows the balance, the money put in and the estimated returns, with a year-by-year table and a How this is calculated panel.

articles.title: How to Estimate How Much You Need to Retire
articles.excerpt: A step-by-step way to estimate the savings needed to cover retirement expenses with inflation, what your savings may grow to, and the monthly saving that closes a gap.
blocks: Retirement planning means setting aside money during working years to cover living costs after work. A rough estimate needs only a few numbers: how long until you retire, how much you save, what it might earn, what you will spend, and how fast prices rise. This guide walks through the sums with an example and explains what the result does and does not tell you. The Retirement Calculator does the same steps and shows each one.
Step 1: what your savings may grow to

Savings grow in two parts: what you already have, and what you add each month. For a 30-year-old who plans to retire at 60, there are 360 months to grow. With ₹5,00,000 saved today and ₹20,000 added each month at an expected 10% a year, the formula Balance = S × (1 + i)^N + C × ((1 + i)^N − 1) ÷ i gives about ₹5,51,28,458.18 at retirement. Here i = 10 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 and N = 360.
Step 2: what your expenses will be

Today's prices will not hold for 30 years. If you need ₹40,000 a month in today's money and prices rise 6% a year, that grows to 40,000 × 1.06^30 = ₹2,29,739.65 a month at age 60. Inflation is the biggest reason a retirement figure that looks large today can fall short later. Inflation is the change in prices for goods and services over time, so a given amount buys less.

The money you hold at retirement has to pay a growing expense for the rest of your plan. If you plan to age 85, that is 25 years, or 300 months. While you spend the money, the rest keeps earning, say 7% a year, and the monthly expense keeps rising with inflation. The corpus needed is the starting expense multiplied by (1 − r^M) ÷ (1 − r), where r = (1 + monthly inflation) ÷ (1 + monthly return) and M = 300. In the example it comes to ₹5,99,08,354.46.

The estimated savings of ₹5,51,28,458.18 are ₹47,79,896.28 short of the ₹5,99,08,354.46 needed. Saving an extra ₹2,114.54 a month, for all 360 months at the same return, would close the gap. A different set of numbers can give a surplus instead. If you saved only ₹1,000 a month in the example, the shortfall would be about ₹4.77 crore, so the monthly amount matters far more than any one assumption.

The age you retire: each extra working year adds contributions and growth and shortens the years to fund
The return before and after retirement: lower returns need a bigger corpus
Inflation: a higher rate raises both your future expenses and the corpus
How long you plan for: living longer than the plan is the main risk of any figure

This is a simple model with a steady return and steady inflation, no tax, no pension, no other income and no change in spending. Real life is less tidy. Use the result as a rough guide to see which numbers matter, and speak to a qualified adviser before making decisions. It is general information, not financial advice.

Official investor-education sites, such as Investor.gov in the United States, offer free calculators for compound interest and savings goals, and it is worth running your plan through more than one tool. If two give very different answers, the inputs are usually different, for example a different return, inflation rate or retirement age. Compare the assumptions before comparing the results.

Ignoring inflation, so the plan is in today's rupees but the bills are in future rupees
Assuming a high return for the whole period
Planning only to a round age such as 75 and then outliving the money
Leaving out healthcare costs and one-off expenses

Enter your age, retirement age and the age you plan to, your savings, monthly saving, expected monthly expenses in today's money, the returns before and after retirement, and inflation. The calculator shows the savings at retirement, the corpus needed, the surplus or shortfall, and the extra monthly saving that closes a shortfall.

articles.title: How Inflation Changes the Value of Money Over Time
articles.excerpt: How to work out what something will cost in future, what a future amount is worth in today's money, and the average inflation rate between two prices, with worked examples.
blocks: Inflation is the change in prices for goods and services over time. When prices rise, the same amount of money buys less than before, which is why economists describe inflation as a fall in the purchasing power of money. This guide shows three calculations: the future cost of something, what a future amount is worth in today's money, and the average inflation rate between two prices. Each has a worked example. The Inflation Calculator does the sums and shows each step.

If prices rise by a steady percentage every year, a cost grows by the same factor each year: Future cost = Cost today × (1 + inflation)^years. At 6% a year, something that costs ₹1,00,000 today costs 1,00,000 × 1.06^10 = ₹1,79,084.77 in 10 years, which is ₹79,084.77 more. After 20 years the same item costs ₹3,20,713.55, more than three times as much.
2. What a future amount is worth today

Run the same sum backwards to see what a future amount could buy in today's prices: Worth today = Future amount ÷ (1 + inflation)^years. At 6% a year, ₹1,00,000 received in 10 years is worth only 1,00,000 ÷ 1.06^10 = ₹55,839.48 in today's money. This is the difference between a nominal value, the number of rupees, and a real value, what those rupees can buy.
3. The average inflation rate between two prices

If you know an old price and a new price and the years between, the average yearly rate is (New ÷ Old)^(1 ÷ years) − 1. For example, if a price rose from ₹100 to ₹179.08 in 10 years, the ratio is 1.7908 and the tenth root is 1.06, so inflation averaged 6% a year. The total rise was 79.08%, which is more than ten times the yearly rate because each year builds on the last. Real years differ: the average hides years with higher and lower rises.

A savings return has to be compared with inflation. If a deposit earns 7% and prices rise 6%, the real gain is only about 1%, because the money buys only about 1% more than before. If prices rise faster than the interest, the money buys less each year even though the balance grows. For long goals such as education or retirement, the future cost of the goal is the number to plan for, not today's price.

Inflation matters most for goals that are years away. A course that costs ₹10,00,000 today and whose fees rise 8% a year would cost 10,00,000 × 1.08^12 = ₹25,18,170 in 12 years. The sum is the same as for any other price, only the rate is different, which is why the calculator lets you choose the rate. The real return on savings is the gap between the interest rate and inflation: a deposit earning 7% while prices rise 6% grows your buying power by about 0.94%, since 1.07 ÷ 1.06 − 1 is 0.0094.

The calculator assumes the same rate every year, but real inflation changes from year to year
Different goods inflate at different rates: education, medical care and food can rise faster or slower than the average
Inflation depends on the basket of goods measured, so a general rate may not match your own spending

Adding the yearly rates instead of compounding them: 6% for 10 years is 79.08%, not 60%
Comparing a future amount with today's price without adjusting for inflation
Using a rate for one item to describe all prices

Choose what to find, enter the amount, the inflation rate or the two prices, and the number of years. The calculator shows the answer and a How this is calculated panel with every step. It does not look up live inflation data, so you enter the rate you want to test.

sources.title: Inflation and price indices, Office for National Statistics

articles.title: Solving for Any Value: A Guide to Time Value of Money
articles.excerpt: How present value, future value, regular deposits, the interest rate and the time are linked by one formula, and how to solve for each in turn, with worked examples.
blocks: Money today is worth more than the same amount later, because today's money can earn interest. This idea, the time value of money, links five numbers: the starting amount, the regular deposit, the final amount, the interest rate and the time. If you know four, you can find the fifth. This guide shows the formula and how to solve for each one, with examples. The Finance Calculator solves any of them and shows the steps.

If an amount is invested at time zero, its value after n periods, the future value, is the start times (1 + i)^n. Discounting reverses this: the present value of an amount due at time n is the amount times (1 + i)^−n. With regular deposits added, the final amount is Final = Start × (1 + i)^n + Deposit × ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i. Here i is the rate for one period, such as the yearly rate ÷ 12 for monthly periods, and n is the number of periods.

To reach ₹10,00,000 in 10 years from nothing at 12% a year, rearrange to Deposit = Final ÷ ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i. With i = 0.01 and n = 120, the divisor is 230.04, so the deposit is about ₹4,347.09 a month.

To reach ₹20,00,000 in 10 years at 12% with ₹5,000 a month, the deposits alone grow to ₹11,50,193.45. The rest must come from the start: Start = (Final − deposits grown) ÷ (1 + i)^n = (20,00,000 − 1,150,193.45) ÷ 3.3004, which is about ₹2,57,486.95.

How long to reach ₹10,00,000 from ₹1,00,000 with ₹5,000 a month at 12%? The number of periods is n = ln((Final × i + D) ÷ (Start × i + D)) ÷ ln(1 + i), where D is the deposit. With i = 0.01 and D = 5,000, n is about 92.1 months, or 7.67 years.

The rate has no direct formula, because i appears in several places. The calculator tries a rate, works out the final amount it gives, and narrows the range until it matches yours. It then checks that the rate reproduces the final amount. The rate cannot be negative here: if the final amount is less than the money you put in, the calculator says so.

Because the five values are linked, every answer can be checked by running the sum the other way. If the calculator says a deposit of ₹4,347.09 a month reaches ₹10,00,000 in 10 years at 12%, put that deposit back in and ask for the final amount: it should return ₹10,00,000. The calculator also does this check when it finds a rate. A mismatch usually means one input was changed between the two runs, such as the number of periods per year or whether deposits are at the start or end of a period.

How often deposits and interest are added: monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or yearly
Whether deposits come at the start or end of each period: at the start each one earns one more period
Whether the rate is a yearly rate divided across the periods, which is the usual way a nominal rate is stated

Mixing a yearly rate with monthly periods without dividing by 12
Entering the time in months when the calculator expects years
Expecting the answer to include tax, fees or inflation, which it does not
Choose what to find, fill in the other values, and read the answer with the steps. The result assumes a steady rate and equal deposits every period, so it is an estimate and not advice.

articles.title: Simple Interest vs Compound Interest: See the Difference
articles.excerpt: How simple and compound interest are worked out, with the same loan or deposit compared side by side, and why compounding earns more the longer money is left.
blocks: Interest is the price of using money. Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount, while compound interest is also calculated on the interest already added. Over short periods the two are close, but over long periods compounding pulls far ahead. This guide shows both formulas with the same numbers so you can see the difference. The Interest Calculator works out both at once and shows the steps.

Simple interest is Interest = P × R × T ÷ 100, where P is the principal, R is the yearly rate in percent and T is the time in years. The interest is the same every year. For ₹1,00,000 at 8% for 10 years, the interest is 1,00,000 × 8 × 10 ÷ 100 = ₹80,000, so the total is ₹1,80,000.

Compound interest adds the interest to the balance every period, so the next period earns interest on a larger amount. The balance is A = P × (1 + r ÷ k)^(k × T), where r is the yearly rate as a fraction and k is how many times a year interest is added. With yearly compounding for the same example, A = 1,00,000 × 1.08^10 = ₹2,15,892.50, so the interest is ₹1,15,892.50. That is ₹35,892.50 more than simple interest.

In year 1 both methods pay ₹8,000. In year 2, simple interest pays ₹8,000 again, while compound interest pays 8% of ₹1,08,000, which is ₹8,640. The gap grows each year because the interest itself earns interest. This is what the time value of money describes: a given sum grows faster the longer it is invested and the more often it is added.

More frequent compounding earns a little more. At 8% for 10 years, compounding monthly instead of yearly gives interest of ₹1,21,964.02 instead of ₹1,15,892.50. The difference is smaller than the jump from simple to compound interest, but it is worth knowing when comparing deposits. Banks often state an effective annual rate for this reason, so offers with different compounding can be compared fairly.

A common shortcut, the rule of 72, says money doubles in about 72 ÷ rate years when interest compounds. At 8% that is 9 years, and 1.08^9 is almost exactly 2. With simple interest at 8%, doubling takes 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 years, because only the original amount earns. The shortcut is only approximate, but it shows the difference between the two methods in one line. The longer the period, the more the gap matters, which is why a young saver gains more from compounding than the same deposit made late.

Most bank deposits and many investments use compound interest
Some short loans, such as some personal arrangements, use simple interest
Credit cards and most long loans compound, though loans are usually charged on a reducing balance
When you borrow, compounding works against you, and when you save it works for you

A small table makes the pattern clear. With simple interest at 8% on ₹1,00,000 the balance is ₹1,08,000 after year 1, ₹1,16,000 after year 2 and ₹1,24,000 after year 3, rising by the same ₹8,000 each time. With yearly compounding it is ₹1,08,000, ₹1,16,640 and ₹1,25,971.20, rising by a larger amount each year. By year 10 the compound balance is well ahead, and by year 30 it is several times the simple one.

Comparing a simple rate with a compound rate as if they were the same thing
Treating a monthly rate as yearly or the other way round
Expecting compounding to matter much over a few months: it matters over years
Forgetting that days and months must be converted to years (1/365 and 1/12) before using the formula

Enter the principal, the yearly rate, the time in years, months or days, and how often compound interest is added. The calculator shows simple and compound interest side by side, with the totals and a How this is calculated panel.
